uncited: The algorithm processes a 3D volume dataset $V$ with dimensions $D_x \times D_y \times D_z$ and a viewing transformation matrix $M_{view}$ to produce a 2D image $I$ of resolution $W \times H$.
For optimization, three Run-Length Encoded (RLE) structures are pre-computed, one for each principal axis (X, Y, Z).
**Intermediate Image ($I_{int}$):** A 2D buffer of size $W \times H$ storing accumulated color $C$ and opacity $\alpha$.
Determine the principal viewing axis (the axis most aligned with the view direction vector $v_o$).
The permutation matrix $P$ reorders coordinates so that the principal axis becomes the Z-axis in the intermediate space.
Compute the shear matrix $S$ to align viewing rays with the principal axis (Z).
Iterate through each slice $z$ of the volume (from front to back in sheared space).
*   Apply the shear transformation to the slice coordinates.
*   Resample the sheared slice into the intermediate image $I_{int}$ using bilinear interpolation.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot W \cdot H)$, where $N$ is the number of slices, and $W \times H$ is the image resolution.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(V + W \cdot H)$, where $V$ is the volume size.

It solves the problem of inefficient memory access and expensive trilinear interpolation in arbitrary viewing angles by transforming the volume into a "sheared object space" where viewing rays are parallel to a coordinate axis and perpendicular to the volume slices [S2, S4, S15, unofficial][S22].

They explicitly state that the algorithm transforms the volume into a 'sheared object space' (or intermediate coordinate system) via a shear transformation. In this space, the viewing rays are made parallel to a coordinate axis (specifically the z-axis or third coordinate axis) and perpendicular to the volume slices. This transformation allows the algorithm to use efficient slice-based compositing (often with bilinear interpolation) instead of expensive trilinear interpolation for every ray in arbitrary viewing angles, thereby solving the problem of inefficient memory access and computational cost associated with standard ray casting.
